questions.stem: Which rule is applied to derive \(B\) from \(A \land B\)?
questions.explanation: Conjunction Elimination (\(\land\text{E}\)) allows us to derive either component of a conjunction. From \(A \land B\), we can derive \(B\) using this rule.

distractorRationale.a: Conjunction Introduction is used to combine two statements, not to derive one from a conjunction.
distractorRationale.c: Implication Introduction is used to discharge assumptions, not to derive components of a conjunction.
distractorRationale.d: Implication Elimination is used to derive a conclusion from an implication, not from a conjunction.

questions.stem: What is the purpose of Implication Introduction (\(\rightarrow\text{I}\)) in natural deduction?
questions.explanation: Implication Introduction (\(\rightarrow\text{I}\)) is used to discharge an assumption, allowing us to conclude an implication from a conditional proof.

distractorRationale.a: Implication Introduction does not introduce new assumptions; it discharges existing ones.
distractorRationale.c: Deriving a conjunction is done using Conjunction Introduction, not Implication Introduction.
distractorRationale.d: Eliminating a disjunction is not related to Implication Introduction.

questions.stem: Explain how assumptions are used and discharged in natural deduction, particularly in the context of proving \(A \rightarrow (B \rightarrow A)\).
markingGuide: Identify that assumptions are temporarily introduced to derive conclusions.
Explain that assumptions are discharged using Implication Introduction.
Describe the specific steps for proving \(A \rightarrow (B \rightarrow A)\).
questions.explanation: In natural deduction, assumptions are used as temporary premises to derive conclusions. They are discharged using Implication Introduction, which allows us to conclude an implication. For \(A \rightarrow (B \rightarrow A)\), we assume \(A\), then assume \(B\), and conclude \(A\). We discharge \(B\) to get \(B \rightarrow A\), and then discharge \(A\) to conclude \(A \rightarrow (B \rightarrow A)\).

distractorRationale.c: This is not a valid deduction; disjunction does not allow direct derivation of one component.

questions.stem: In the proof of \(P \rightarrow (Q \rightarrow P)\), which assumption is discharged first?
questions.explanation: In the proof of \(P \rightarrow (Q \rightarrow P)\), we first assume \(P\), then \(Q\). After deriving \(P\), we discharge \(Q\) to conclude \(Q \rightarrow P\), and then discharge \(P\) to conclude \(P \rightarrow (Q \rightarrow P)\).

distractorRationale.a: P is discharged after Q, as it is the outer assumption.
distractorRationale.c: P \land Q is not an assumption in this proof.
distractorRationale.d: Assumptions are discharged in this proof; Q is discharged first.

questions.explanation: Introduction rules in natural deduction allow us to introduce logical connectives into a proof, such as using Conjunction Introduction to combine two statements. Elimination rules allow us to remove or use logical connectives, such as using Implication Elimination to derive a conclusion from an implication. These rules are essential for constructing valid proofs.

questions.stem: In natural deduction, every assumption must be discharged by the end of the proof.
questions.explanation: In natural deduction, all assumptions must be discharged by the end of the proof to ensure that the conclusion is validly derived from the premises without relying on any undischarged assumptions.

distractorRationale.b: In natural deduction, it is essential to discharge all assumptions to ensure the proof is valid and complete.
